Unlike standard Iterated Function Systems (IFS) which require recursive traversal and cause divergent control flow, KRS uses a fixed operation count logarithmic time algorithm, allowing efficient parallelization [S1].

The evidence explicitly states in the notes and passages that 'Unlike standard IFS which requires recursive traversal and causes divergent control flow on GPUs, KRS uses a fixed operation count logarithmic time algorithm without recursion, allowing efficient GPU sphere tracing.' This directly supports every part of the claim: the contrast with standard IFS (recursive/divergent), the nature of KRS (fixed operation count/logarithmic time/no recursion), and the result (efficient parallelization/GPU sphere tracing).
supported
The method can handle any Lipschitz transformation by sacrificing performance [S1].

The claim is directly supported by the text in Source [S1], specifically in section '5.2. Distance distortion'. The text states: 'By sacrificing some performance, we can handle any Lipschitz transformation of the KRS geometry as described by Hart [Har96].' This matches the claim's assertion that the method handles any Lipschitz transformation by sacrificing performance.

Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) are a procedural modeling technique for generating complex, fractal-like geometries using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and reflection transformations [S1].

The claim states that Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) are a procedural modeling technique for generating complex, fractal-like geometries using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and reflection transformations. Source [S1] explicitly defines KRS as a 'procedural modeling approach' composed of 'kernel geometries defined by signed distance functions, and reflection transformations'. It further describes the generation of geometries through recursive expansion levels involving unions of kernels and reflected previous levels, which creates fractal-like structures. The source confirms the use of SDFs for distance evaluation and reflection operators for transformation, directly supporting every part of the claim.

This is equivalent to discarding the part of the geometry on the positive side, providing an underestimation for the distance to the mirrored geometry, which remains suitable for sphere tracing [S1].

The claim is explicitly stated in the source text. Specifically, in the passage discussing the distance function evaluation when a geometry intersects the mirror plane, the text says: 'Note that if Ai is not entirely on the negative side, but intersected by the mirror plane, we can still apply the same formula. Doing so is equivalent to discarding the part of the geometry on the positive side. We obtain an underestimation for the distance to the mirrored geometry, which is still suitable for sphere tracing.' This matches the claim word-for-word in meaning and fact.
